index.title: Designing structures with rfd4-generate
index.intro: RFD4-Proteina starts from noise and turns it into a protein. You tell it what to keep, what to build, and how long to make it, and it gives you back structures. This site walks through one run at a time, using real output from runs on our own machine.
index.oneCommand: There are two commands to learn. rfd4-generate makes designs. rfd4-evaluate scores them. Everything else is options on those two.
index.stepsTitle: What happens when you press return
index.runs: Each one is a real run. The command that made it is on its page, so you can see exactly what produced the structures you are looking at.
index.counts: RFD4 finishes every sample it starts, so there is no funnel of survivors the way there is in BindCraft2. The question is not how many got through, it is how many were worth keeping.
index.vsTitle: Next to BindCraft2 in one table
index.vs: You have already used BindCraft2 on this course. These two tools look similar from the outside and work very differently inside.
rfd4.vs.start.rfd4: Noise. The model draws a structure out of it.
rfd4.vs.start.bc2: A target structure and a prediction network it pushes around.
rfd4.vs.input.rfd4: A condition spec: a contig string and a set of conditions.
rfd4.vs.input.bc2: A settings JSON file with a target and hotspots in it.
rfd4.vs.aim.rfd4: Conditions on atoms and residues, from hotspots to hydrogen bonding to a fold label.
rfd4.vs.aim.bc2: Hotspot and coldspot residue lists, plus a modality.
rfd4.vs.judge.rfd4: Nothing, unless you ask. Scoring is a separate step you turn on.
rfd4.vs.judge.bc2: Filters after every stage, so a bad attempt is dropped as it goes.
rfd4.vs.out.rfd4: CIF structures, and a metrics table if you asked for one.
rfd4.vs.out.bc2: Trajectories, refolded candidates and a ranked table.
rfd4.vs.time.rfd4: Sixty model evaluations per design, so a design is quick.
rfd4.vs.fail.rfd4: It will happily hand you a structure nothing can fold. With metrics off, nothing tells you.
rfd4.vs.time.bc2: Minutes per trajectory on our hardware, and most trajectories are thrown away.
rfd4.vs.fail.bc2: It can pass its own filters on an interface that is not real.
process.title: How a run works
process.intro: A run is sixty passes through the model. Each pass moves the structure a little further from noise and a little closer to something protein shaped. Nothing is discarded along the way, which is the big difference from BindCraft2.
process.steps: Drag the slider to walk through the steps. Early on the chain is barely a chain. By the end the backbone is laid down and the sequence has been chosen with it.
process.stepsNote: This is a drawing, not captured data. The real frames from a real run are on the trajectory page.
process.whatTitle: The options that change what the sampler does
process.what: These are the ones worth knowing. Every value here is RFD4's own default, so anything you do not set is what you see below.
process.pipeline: Each phase writes files. Knowing which file comes from which phase is most of what you need when a run goes wrong.
process.not: Four things people expect from it that it will not do for you.
process.not.filter: It does not throw away bad designs. Every sample you ask for is written out.
process.not.mpnn: It does not run a separate sequence design step. Sequence and structure come out together.
process.not.rank: It does not rank anything. The metrics table is a table, not an order of merit.
process.not.affinity: It does not predict binding affinity. Nothing here tells you a binder will bind.
knob.nsteps: How many passes through the model. Fewer is faster and rougher.
knob.guidance_w: How hard the model is pushed towards your conditions. Above 1 follows them more closely and explores less.
knob.recycle_strategy: How much the model reconsiders its own output as it goes.
knob.n_recycle: Extra recycling passes on top of the strategy.
knob.batch_size: How many designs run together on the card. Bigger uses more memory.
knob.num_replicates: How many designs to make per entry in your spec file.
knob.generation: The sampler to use. inverse_folding holds the backbone and only changes the sequence.
knob.inference_backend: Which implementation runs the model. Leave it alone unless you are chasing speed.
phase.spec: You describe the design you want
phase.load: RFD4 resolves your command into one config
phase.sample: The model turns noise into a structure, step by step
phase.metrics: Each design is measured, if you asked for metrics
phase.refold: A structure predictor is asked whether it agrees
spec.title: Describe the design
spec.intro: This is the part you have to learn. A spec file says which bit of an input structure to keep, how much new protein to build, and what the new protein has to do. Everything else is details.
spec.why: Get this wrong and RFD4 either stops with an error or, worse, designs something other than what you meant. The boxes below check what you type against the rules in the documentation.
spec.examples: Pick one, then change it. Each of these is a spec RFD4 would accept, checked by the test suite that ships with this site.
spec.contig: The contig is a comma separated list read left to right. A token with a chain letter in front keeps part of your input. A bare number builds that many new residues. /0 starts a new chain.
spec.cond: Conditions are how you aim the model. Each one names what to condition on, the value to hold, and the atoms or residues it applies to. This box takes JSON, which the documentation says works wherever YAML does, and the YAML beside it is written from what you type.
spec.condTableTitle: Every condition, and what it does
spec.sel: Every condition points at atoms with a selection. The path form has four fields in a fixed order: chain, residue name, residue number, atom name. Anything you leave off the end means everything.
spec.selTrap: The fields are positional, so an atom name in the third slot is read as a residue number and the run fails with a confusing error. If you want atom N, write sel('B/*/*/N'), with three slashes.
spec.noProblems: Nothing wrong with this that the site can see.
tok.preservedRange: Keep residues 17 to 131 of chain A exactly as they are in the input.
tok.preservedOne: Keep just residue 52 of chain A.
tok.expandRange: Build somewhere between 50 and 120 new residues. The exact length is chosen when the design runs.
tok.named: The same as a bare range, but named, so a condition can select it by name.
tok.namedType: A named segment of exactly 10 residues, made RNA rather than protein by the trailing R.
tok.break: End this chain and start a new one. The new chain gets its own identifier.
cond.C_CRD: Hold these atoms at the coordinates they have in the input. This is how you pin geometry.
cond.C_SEQ: Hold the residue identity these residues have in the input. This is how you pin sequence.
cond.C_HOT: Mark these atoms as the place you want contacted. The closest thing to a BindCraft2 hotspot.
cond.C_RAS: Ask for these atoms to end up buried, exposed, or in between.
cond.C_HB: Ask these atoms to donate a hydrogen bond, accept one, or do both in different bonds.
cond.C_PISTACK: Ask for a stacked aromatic ring. It applies to whole rings, not single atoms.
cond.C_PICATION: Ask for a ring and cation pair, naming which side these atoms are.
cond.C_CATH: Ask for a fold, by its CATH class, architecture and topology. Use x for a level you want left open.
cond.C_CENTROID: Put a whole chain's centre at a position you name. All chains get one or none do.
cond.C_IDX: Put selections into the same index group, so the model treats them as one numbering.
cond.C_CRDGRP: Hold a set of atoms rigid with respect to each other while letting them move as a unit. Clear any absolute coordinates with C_CRD: false first.
cond.C_SEQ_PROB: Set how likely a residue type is at these positions. Zero forbids it outright, which is how you ask for no cysteines.
example.binder: The example out of the documentation, pointed at our own target. The whole target is held by its backbone atoms and its sequence, and a new chain of 50 to 120 residues is built beside it. No face is picked, so the model chooses where to bind.
example.hotspot: The same design with a face named. Marking residues as hotspots tells the model where you want contact, which usually raises your hit rate and narrows what you get.
example.motif: Three residues held in place while the model builds a protein around them. There is no second chain here, so the motif ends up inside one new protein rather than across an interface.
example.nocys: A binder against the bat IL-15 structure, with cysteine forbidden in the designed chain. This is the no disulfides request, which in BindCraft2 was a property flag and here is a sequence probability of zero.
example.rigid: The motif held as a group rather than at fixed coordinates, so the three residues keep their arrangement but can sit anywhere. Note the C_CRD: false that has to come first.
example.invfold: No contig at all. The backbone is taken as given and only the sequence is resampled, which is what generation=inverse_folding does.
command.title: Write the command
command.intro: RFD4 is driven by Hydra, so the command line is a list of key=value pairs. There are no flags with dashes, which catches almost everyone out once.
command.hydra: A plus in front adds a key that has no default. A tilde deletes one. A list value needs quotes round it or the shell takes the brackets apart first.
command.hint: Type a command and press Run. Nothing below changes until you do.
command.ok: This command parses. Everything below is what it would do.
command.tidy: Written out in the order the documentation uses, the same command is:
command.effectTitle: What this run will and will not give you
command.effect: These follow from the options you set, and from the ones you left alone.
command.filesTitle: The files it would leave behind
command.files: Knowing where output lands saves a lot of hunting. The example name is whatever you called the design in your spec file.
command.hydraOut: The resolved config goes to ./hydra_outputs, which is beside your working directory and not inside out_dir. People look for it in the run folder and do not find it.
command.settingsTitle: Every option this run will use
command.settings: The options you set, plus the ones that matter most and their defaults. The last column says where each value came from.
run.title: Run it
run.intro: A real run on our own machine, with the command that made it and the log it printed. Nothing here is a mock up.
run.command: Copy it, change one thing, and you have your own run. Every option on it is explained on the command page.
run.log: The real output. Worth reading once end to end, because the lines that matter when something fails are not the loud ones.
run.counts: Designs asked for, designs written, and how many cleared whatever bar we set. The bar is ours, not RFD4's.
run.files: Worked out from the command, so it matches what you would find if you went looking.
run.notParsed: This run's command does not parse with the options this site knows about, so the notes below are left off.
run.noCounts: No counts were recorded for this run.
trajectory.title: Watch it fold
trajectory.intro: These are the real intermediate structures from a run, saved every few steps. You are watching the model talk itself out of noise.
trajectory.read: Early frames are not bad proteins, they are not proteins at all. Watch where the structure commits, because that is usually much earlier than you expect.
trajectory.noisy: If the run also saved the noisy states, each clean frame has a messier twin: the thing the model was actually handed at that step, as opposed to its guess at the answer.
trajectory.howTitle: How to get frames out of your own run
trajectory.how: Nothing is saved by default. Two options have to be set, and the second one is the one people forget.
traj.every: Save a snapshot every this many steps. Zero, the default, saves nothing at all.
traj.caOnly: Left true, you get alpha carbons only in a binary file. Set it false for all atom frames you can open anywhere.
traj.noisy: Also save the noisy state at each snapshot, beside the clean prediction.
designs.title: Look at the designs
designs.intro: The structures RFD4 wrote, as it wrote them. These are the files you would hand to anything downstream.
designs.cif: RFD4 writes CIF, never PDB. Anything in your pipeline that only reads PDB needs a conversion step put in front of it.
designs.confLegend: coloured by the confidence in the B factor column, blue is low and red is high
designs.list: Every design from every captured run, with whatever was measured on it.
metrics.title: Read the metrics
metrics.intro: RFD4 will measure its designs for you, but only if you ask. This page is one real metrics table, read column by column.
metrics.off: No metrics_tags means no metrics file. A run finishes perfectly happily and tells you nothing about what it made.
metrics.tableTitle: The table as RFD4 wrote it
metrics.table: One row per design. The config columns are hidden here and shown further down, because there are a lot of them.
metrics.chart: Sorting a column is the quickest way to see whether a run gave you a few good designs or a flat field of mediocre ones.
metrics.glossary: The ones worth knowing. A column RFD4 wrote that is not described here still shows in the table above.
metrics.config: RFD4 writes the config into the metrics file, which makes it the run's own record of itself. If you lose track of what made a set of designs, look here.
metrics.noNumbers: No numeric column was found in this file.
metrics.noConfig: This file has no config columns in it.
metric.plddt: The model's confidence in its own local geometry, per residue and averaged. High means the model thinks it knows what it drew, not that it is right.
metric.ptm: Confidence in the overall shape being one coherent thing.
metric.pae: Expected error, in angstroms, in the position of one residue relative to another. Low across an interface is the interesting case.
metric.rmsd: How far one structure sits from another once they are lined up. Which two depends on the column.
metric.tm_score: A shape similarity score that cares about fold rather than exact atoms. Above 0.5 is usually the same fold.
metric.sc_rmsd: Self consistency: predict the design's own sequence back into a structure and see how far it moved. The single most useful number here.
metric.self_consistency: The family of checks that fold the designed sequence again and compare. A design its own sequence will not fold back to is a design to drop.
metric.radius_of_gyration: How spread out the structure is. A surprisingly high value usually means something unfolded.
metric.n_residues: How many residues ended up in the design, which for an expandable contig is chosen at run time.
metric.seed: The random seed. Without it in the file you cannot reproduce a design.
metric.length: The designed length for this row.
guidance.title: Steer the model
guidance.intro: Four ways to push a run somewhere specific: start from a structure instead of noise, keep a backbone and change its sequence, lean on a metric while sampling, or search over several attempts and keep the best.
guidance.partialTitle: Partial diffusion: start from something you have
guidance.partial: Instead of starting from noise, hand RFD4 a structure and tell it to redo only the last part of the trajectory. A small fraction stays close to what you gave it. A large one redraws most of it.
guidance.fracLabel: fraction of the trajectory to redo
guidance.notTime: The documentation is firm about one thing here: the step you restart at is not a diffusion time. If you want to set the time itself there are separate options for that, and they take a number between 0 and 1 on a different scale.
guidance.invfoldTitle: Inverse folding: keep the backbone, change the sequence
guidance.invfold: The backbone is held and the sequence and side chains are sampled again. This is what you reach for when you like a shape and want other ways to build it.
guidance.metric: RFD4 can let a metric pull on the sampling as it goes, rather than only judging the result. The options live under +guidance and have no default group, so nothing happens unless you add one.
guidance.metricCaution: This site does not teach the guidance options in detail, because the documentation covers them only in outline and we have not run them here. Read the metric guidance page in the RFD4 documentation before you rely on them.
guidance.search: Rather than one trajectory, run several, score them part way through with a structure predictor, keep the best few and branch again. The picture below shows the shape of it with RFD4's defaults.
guidance.searchCost: Search multiplies your compute by the beam width times the branching, and it needs a structure prediction environment installed. Worth knowing about, worth leaving off until a run matters.
guidance.opt.generation: Switches the sampler to inverse folding.
guidance.opt.tsr_k: How tightly the sequence sampling is held to the backbone. Lower explores more.
guidance.opt.tsr_sigma: The spread allowed in the same sampling.
guidance.opt.beam_width: How many candidate trajectories are kept at each round.
guidance.opt.n_branch: How many new branches each kept candidate spawns.
guidance.opt.save_rollouts: Keep the branches that were dropped, for looking at afterwards.
compare.title: Compare with BindCraft2
compare.intro: You have run BindCraft2 already. Putting the two side by side is the fastest way to understand what each one is actually for.
compare.table: None of these rows is a verdict. They are the places where the two tools make different bets.
compare.same: Numbers from runs against one shared structure, so the comparison is not a comparison of two different problems.
compare.when: A rough rule, which you should argue with once you have used both.
compare.when.rfd4: Reach for RFD4 when the shape is the question: scaffolding a motif, building a fold, making many different backbones quickly.
compare.when.bc2: Reach for BindCraft2 when binding is the question and you want a tool that throws away its own failures before you see them.
compare.when.both: Using both is reasonable. Generate backbones with RFD4, then put the ones you like through a binder pipeline that filters hard.
